You are a Phase 5 compat-timing worker for gba-emu. Your testcase: **heartwrench-gameplay** (video 0.577, audio 0.554).

Branch: `git switch -c phase5/heartwrench-gameplay` in your worktree. Start from main commit 9848efd2692ff83565b65b19897a9348f7974551 (`git reset --hard 9848efd` first if your worktree is on another commit).

Read CLAUDE.md, PLAN.md (Phase 5) and your agent definition; they are binding.

**Files you may edit (assigned by the integrator):** src/bus.rs (wait states, Game Pak prefetch buffer) and src/cart.rs (save memory: the ROM declares SRAM_V). Two other workers own other files in parallel: one has the CPU timing files (cpu/*.rs), the other ppu/bg_text.rs and ppu/effects.rs. Touch nothing else. If the cause is elsewhere, report it with evidence instead of editing.

**Integrator triage:** heartwrench matches the reference closely up to about frame 2900, apart from the very first frames. Then the player's position drifts: in the same rooms the character stands in different places. The error rises around frames 3900-6600 and the run re-converges near the end. That points to accumulated timing drift. The game probably runs from Game Pak ROM with WAITCNT set to 0x4317 and prefetch on. The bus implements WAITCNT wait states and sequential/non-sequential timing, but no Game Pak prefetch buffer: `ponytail:` in bus.rs WaitStates::access_cost. So with prefetch enabled, ROM code is charged far more cycles than on hardware. Implement the prefetch buffer per gbatek "GBA GamePak Prefetch" (in GBA System Control). Keep it fast: the bus is the hottest path. Also check that SRAM saves behave per gbatek "GBA Cartridge Backup Media" (8-bit only, 32K/64K). Check that heartwrench improves and nothing in the procedural set regresses. The timer-reload and timer-start-stop delay constants were tuned against current timing, so if they drop, report it (don't edit timer.rs).

Method:
- Run every grader under the shared lock, one at a time:
  `flock /tmp/claude-1000/-var-www-html-test-projects-gba-trial-gba-emu/ec739230-fb4b-467b-9709-e53c38e370f4/scratchpad/grader.lock scripts/grade-subset.sh ...`
- For video, see the integrator's example in `/tmp/claude-1000/-var-www-html-test-projects-gba-trial-gba-emu/ec739230-fb4b-467b-9709-e53c38e370f4/scratchpad/triage5/` (a docker grader run with `--emit-video` on a 1-testcase corpus in sub/).
- The per-testcase JSON has `audit_luma_mae_frames` (per-frame error) to locate the divergence.

Report the first diverging frame before and after. Grade: `heartwrench-gameplay spout-gameplay` plus the full procedural set `aw-arm-alu aw-arm-ldr-str aw-arm-ldm-stm aw-thumb-alu aw-thumb-ldr-str aw-thumb-ldm-stm memory mgba-io-read mgba-shifter mgba-carry mgba-dma timer-reload timer-start-stop dma-priority ppu-vram-mirror tonc-snd1`, before and after. Done checklist (CLAUDE.md). Commit in small Conventional Commits; never push. Report per your agent definition.

# gba-emu: rules for every agent

Read PLAN.md before starting. It defines the phases, the shared contracts and who owns which file.
The benchmark lives at `/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-eval`, referred to below as `$GBA_EVAL`.
Use that absolute path; relative paths break inside worktrees.

## Originality (hard rule)
- Write all code yourself. Do not read, copy, or paraphrase any existing emulator:
  `$GBA_EVAL/candidates/` (gba-core), `$GBA_EVAL/third_party/` (Mesen2),
  `$GBA_EVAL/reference/mesen_step.cpp`, or mGBA/NanoBoyAdvance/VBA/etc. from memory or the web.
- Allowed sources: `$GBA_EVAL/spec/gbatek.htm` (GBA, ARM and THUMB chapters only), `$GBA_EVAL/spec/ABI.md`,
  `$GBA_EVAL/spec/gba_bios_stub.h`, the grader's outputs (scores, `.ref.png` vs `.cand.png`),
  and running ROMs from `$GBA_EVAL/corpus/roms/`.
- No per-ROM hacks: never branch on a ROM's hash, title, or game code. Fix the hardware behavior.

## Code readability
- Use clear, descriptive names for functions, variables and types: `destination_register`, `shift_amount`,
  `fn execute_data_processing`. Never cryptic ones like `x`, `t`, `rd2` or `tmp`. Loop indices
  (`i`, `line`) are fine when the meaning is obvious.
- Official gbatek register and field names are allowed (`DISPCNT`, `BG0CNT`, `IE`, `IF`, `CPSR`, `Rd`, `Rn`),
  each with a short plain-English comment where it is defined, e.g. `const DISPCNT: u32 = 0x000; // display control`.
- Every non-obvious function gets a one-line doc comment naming the gbatek section it implements, e.g.
  `/// Barrel shifter for data-processing operand 2 (gbatek: ARM Opcodes: Data Processing (ALU)).`
- Prefer small readable functions over clever one-liners. Split a long `match` arm or a dense bit-twiddling
  expression into a named helper.

## Ownership
- Only edit the files your task owns (see the ownership tables in PLAN.md).
- Shared files (`src/lib.rs`, `src/gba.rs`, `src/bus.rs`, `src/io.rs`, `src/irq.rs`, `src/scheduler.rs`,
  `Cargo.toml`) are changed only by the integrator (the executor session). If you need a contract
  change, say so in your report instead of making it.

## Git
- Remote: https://github.com/Rohan-Jalil/gba-eval-trial-rohan. Never push; the human pushes.
- Author and committer: Rohan Jalil <[REDACTED:email]>. This is set in this repo's git config;
  do not override it.
- Use Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary`, for example `feat(cpu): add ARM data-processing ops`,
  `fix(ppu): wrap affine BG coordinates`, `test(timer): cascade overflow`, `docs(notes): phase 1 decisions`,
  `chore(results): phase 1 milestone`. Scopes: cpu, arm, thumb, bus, io, irq, ppu, apu, dma, timer,
  keypad, cart, abi, scripts, plan, notes, results.
- Commit after every meaningful step (a working instruction group, a passing test, a merged branch),
  not one large commit per phase.
- Worker agents commit on their own branch. Only the integrator merges into `main` (`git merge --no-ff`).

## Logging
- `NOTES.md`: add an entry for every decision or change of approach (date, what, why), and for every
  phase record which agents ran and on which model. The integrator writes the agent/model rows.
- `TIMELOG.md` belongs to the human. Agents never edit it.
- Milestones: `scripts/grade-full.sh <phase> "<note>"` saves `results/milestones/<phase>/`. Commit that
  folder and `scores.tsv`. All other `results/` output stays ignored.

## Before you report done
1. `cargo test` passes.
2. `cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` succeeds.
3. `scripts/grade-subset.sh target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm <name> <your tests> <smoke set>`.
   Report the per-test scores, and never lower a smoke-set score without saying so.
4. Your work is committed on your branch, and your report lists the commits.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips

//! System bus: memory map, region dispatch and access-cycle costs (gbatek: GBA Memory Map).
//!
//! The CPU only ever talks to the bus. Every access adds its cycle cost to `access_cycles`,
//! which the CPU drains with `take_access_cycles()` to report how long a step took.

use crate::apu::Apu;
use crate::cart::Cart;
use crate::dma::Dma;
use crate::io::SerialStub;
use crate::irq::Irq;
use crate::keypad::Keypad;
use crate::ppu::Ppu;
use crate::timer::Timers;

/// The 16 KiB BIOS stub supplied by the benchmark, mapped at 0x00000000.
static BIOS: &[u8; BIOS_SIZE] = include_bytes!("../assets/gba_bios_stub.bin");

pub const BIOS_SIZE: usize = 0x4000;
pub const EWRAM_SIZE: usize = 0x40000; // on-board work RAM, 256 KiB
pub const IWRAM_SIZE: usize = 0x8000; // on-chip work RAM, 32 KiB

/// Access width, used to pick the cycle cost.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
pub enum Width {
    Byte,
    Halfword,
    Word,
}

/// Memory regions, selected by address bits 24-27.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
enum Region {
    Bios,
    Ewram,
    Iwram,
    Io,
    Palette,
    Vram,
    Oam,
    Rom,
    Sram,
    Unmapped,
}

fn region_of(address: u32) -> Region {
    match address >> 24 {
        0x00 => Region::Bios,
        0x02 => Region::Ewram,
        0x03 => Region::Iwram,
        0x04 => Region::Io,
        0x05 => Region::Palette,
        0x06 => Region::Vram,
        0x07 => Region::Oam,
        0x08..=0x0D => Region::Rom,
        0x0E | 0x0F => Region::Sram,
        _ => Region::Unmapped,
    }
}

/// Wait-state settings derived from WAITCNT (0x4000204) and the internal memory control register
/// (0x4000800) (gbatek: GBA System Control). All values are total cycles for one 16-bit access.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
pub struct WaitStates {
    /// Game Pak ROM wait states 0-2: first (non-sequential) access.
    rom_nonsequential: [u32; 3],
    /// Game Pak ROM wait states 0-2: second (sequential) access.
    rom_sequential: [u32; 3],

areas are called Wait State 0-2. Different access timings may be assigned to
each area (this might be useful in case that a game pak contains several ROM
chips with different access times each).

  Bit   Expl.
  0-1   SRAM Wait Control          (0..3 = 4,3,2,8 cycles)
  2-3   Wait State 0 First Access  (0..3 = 4,3,2,8 cycles)
  4     Wait State 0 Second Access (0..1 = 2,1 cycles)
  5-6   Wait State 1 First Access  (0..3 = 4,3,2,8 cycles)
  7     Wait State 1 Second Access (0..1 = 4,1 cycles; unlike above WS0)
  8-9   Wait State 2 First Access  (0..3 = 4,3,2,8 cycles)
  10    Wait State 2 Second Access (0..1 = 8,1 cycles; unlike above WS0,WS1)
  11-12 PHI Terminal Output        (0..3 = Disable, 4.19MHz, 8.38MHz, 16.78MHz)
  13    Not used
  14    Game Pak Prefetch Buffer (Pipe) (0=Disable, 1=Enable)
  15    Game Pak Type Flag  (Read Only) (0=GBA, 1=CGB) (IN35 signal)
  16-31 Not used

At startup, the default setting is 0000h. Currently manufactured cartridges are
using the following settings: WS0/ROM=3,1 clks; SRAM=8 clks; WS2/EEPROM: 8,8
clks; prefetch enabled; that is, WAITCNT=4317h, for more info see "GBA
Cartridges" chapter.

First Access (Non-sequential) and Second Access (Sequential) define the
waitstates for N and S cycles, the actual access time is 1 clock cycle PLUS the
number of waitstates.
GamePak uses 16bit data bus, so that a 32bit access is split into TWO 16bit
accesses (of which, the second fragment is always sequential, even if the first
fragment was non-sequential).

GBA GamePak Prefetch

NOTES:
The GBA forcefully uses non-sequential timing at the beginning of each
128K-block of gamepak ROM, eg. "LDMIA [801fff8h],r0-r7" will have
non-sequential timing at 8020000h.
The PHI Terminal output (PHI Pin of Gamepak Bus) should be disabled.

4000300h - POSTFLG - BYTE - Undocumented - Post Boot / Debug Control (R/W)
After initial reset, the GBA BIOS initializes the register to 01h, and any
further execution of the Reset vector (00000000h) will pass control to the
Debug vector (0000001Ch) when sensing the register to be still set to 01h.

  Bit   Expl.
  0     Undocumented. First Boot Flag  (0=First, 1=Further)
  1-7   Undocumented. Not used.

Normally the debug handler rejects control unless it detects Debug flags in
cartridge header, in that case it may redirect to a cut-down boot procedure
(bypassing Nintendo logo and boot delays, much like nocash burst boot for
multiboot software). I am not sure if it is possible to reset the GBA
externally without automatically resetting register 300h though.

4000301h - HALTCNT - BYTE - Undocumented - Low Power Mode Control (W)
Writing to this register switches the GBA into battery saving mode.
In Halt mode, the CPU is paused as long as (IE AND IF)=0, this should be used
to reduce power-consumption during periods when the CPU is waiting for
interrupt events.
In Stop mode, most of the hardware including sound and video are paused, this
very-low-power mode could be used much like a screensaver.

  Bit   Expl.
  0-6   Undocumented. Not used.
  7     Undocumented. Power Down Mode  (0=Halt, 1=Stop)

The current GBA BIOS addresses only the upper eight bits of this register (by
writing 00h or 80h to address 04000301h), however, as the register isn't
officially documented, some or all of the bits might have different meanings in
future GBA models.
For best forwards compatibility, it'd generally be more recommended to use the
BIOS Functions SWI 2 (Halt) or SWI 3 (Stop) rather than writing to this
register directly.

4000410h - Undocumented - Purpose Unknown ? 8bit (W)
The BIOS writes the 8bit value 0FFh to this address. Purpose Unknown.
Probably just another bug in the BIOS.

4000800h - 32bit - Undocumented - Internal Memory Control (R/W)
Supported by GBA and GBA SP only - NOT supported by DS (even in GBA mode).
Also supported by GBA Micro - but crashes on "overclocked" WRAM setting.
Initialized to 0D000020h (by hardware). Unlike all other I/O registers, this
register is mirrored across the whole I/O area (in increments of 64K, ie. at
4000800h, 4010800h, 4020800h, ..., 4FF0800h)

  Bit   Expl.
  0     Disable 32K+256K WRAM (0=Normal, 1=Disable) (when off: empty/prefetch)
         From endrift: bit0 swaps 00000000h-01FFFFFFh and 02000000h-03FFFFFFh
         in GBA mode (but keeps BIOS protection)
  1     Unknown          (Read/Write-able)
  2     Unknown          (Read/Write-able)
  3     Disable CGB Bootrom (0=Normal, 1=Disable, start cart at 0000h)
  4     Unused (0)
  5     Enable 256K WRAM (0=Disable, 1=Normal) (when off: mirror of 32K WRAM)
  6-23  Unused (0)
  24-27 Wait Control WRAM 256K (0-14 = 15..1 Waitstates, 15=Lockup)
  28-31 Unknown          (Read/Write-able)

The default value 0Dh in Bits 24-27 selects 2 waitstates for 256K WRAM (ie.
3/3/6 cycles 8/16/32bit accesses). The fastest possible setting would be 0Eh (1
waitstate, 2/2/4 cycles for 8/16/32bit), that works on GBA and GBA SP only, the
GBA Micro locks up with that setting (it's on-chip RAM is too slow, and works
only with 2 or more waitstates).

Note: One cycle equals approx. 59.59ns (ie. 16.78MHz clock).





  
  GBA GamePak Prefetch

GamePak Prefetch can be enabled in WAITCNT register. When prefetch buffer is
enabled, the GBA attempts to read opcodes from Game Pak ROM during periods when
the CPU is not using the bus (if any). Memory access is then performed with 0
Waits if the CPU requests data which is already stored in the buffer. The
prefetch buffer stores up to eight 16bit values.

GamePak ROM Opcodes
The prefetch feature works only with <opcodes> fetched from GamePak ROM.
Opcodes executed in RAM or BIOS are not affected by the prefetch feature (even
if that opcodes read <data> from GamePak ROM).

Prefetch Enable
For GamePak ROM opcodes, prefetch may occur in two situations:

  1) opcodes with internal cycles (I) which do not change R15, shift/rotate
     register-by-register, load opcodes (ldr,ldm,pop,swp), multiply opcodes
  2) opcodes that load/store memory (ldr,str,ldm,stm,etc.)


Prefetch Disable Bug
When Prefetch is disabled, the Prefetch Disable Bug will occur for all

  "Opcodes in GamePak ROM with Internal Cycles which do not change R15"

for those opcodes, the bug changes the opcode fetch time from 1S to 1N.
Note: Affected opcodes (with I cycles) are: Shift/rotate register-by-register
opcodes, multiply opcodes, and load opcodes (ldr,ldm,pop,swp).





  
  GBA Cartridges

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Fast feedback: grade a wasm against only the testcases you name.
#
#   scripts/grade-subset.sh <wasm> <run-name> <testcase-id>...
#   scripts/grade-subset.sh target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm cpu aw-arm-alu mgba-carry
#
# Builds a throwaway corpus (filtered testcases.json + the real ROMs,
# replays and reference cache mounted read-only) and runs the same
# gba-eval-grader docker image as the full grade. Results land in
# results/<run-name>/ in this repo. Section scores in summary.json are
# meaningless for a subset (missing subsystems count as 0); read the
# per-testcase entries instead.
set -euo pipefail

GBA_EVAL="${GBA_EVAL:-/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-eval}"
[ $# -ge 3 ] || { sed -n '2,12p' "$0"; exit 2; }
WASM="$(cd "$(dirname "$1")" && pwd)/$(basename "$1")"; NAME="$2"; shift 2
[ -f "$WASM" ] || { echo "error: $WASM not found" >&2; exit 1; }

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
OUT="$ROOT/results/$NAME"; SUBSET="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$SUBSET"' EXIT
mkdir -p "$OUT"

python3 -I - "$GBA_EVAL/corpus/testcases.json" "$SUBSET/testcases.json" "$@" <<'PY'
import json, sys
src, dst, *ids = sys.argv[1:]
data = json.load(open(src))
cases = data if isinstance(data, list) else data["testcases"]
picked = [c for c in cases if c["id"] in ids]
missing = set(ids) - {c["id"] for c in picked}
if missing:
    sys.exit(f"unknown testcase id(s): {', '.join(sorted(missing))}")
json.dump(picked if isinstance(data, list) else {**data, "testcases": picked}, open(dst, "w"), indent=1)
PY
cp "$GBA_EVAL/corpus/grader.yaml" "$SUBSET/"

docker run --rm \
    -v "$GBA_EVAL":/repo:ro \
    -v "$SUBSET":/subset \
    -v "$GBA_EVAL/corpus/roms":/subset/roms:ro \
    -v "$GBA_EVAL/corpus/replays":/subset/replays:ro \
    -v "$GBA_EVAL/corpus/reference-cache":/subset/reference-cache:ro \
    -v "$(dirname "$WASM")":/wasm:ro \
    -v "$OUT":/out \
    gba-eval-grader /wasm/"$(basename "$WASM")" /subset/ /out

python3 -I - "$OUT" <<'PY'
import json, sys
s = json.load(open(f"{sys.argv[1]}/summary.json"))
for tc, r in sorted(s["per_testcase"].items()):
    print(f"{tc:28} video={r.get('video_score')!s:22} audio={r.get('audio_score')}")
PY

fr

heartwrench-gameplay-strip.png
later.png
log.txt
out

content.content:
GBA Cart Backup IDs

Nintendo didn't include a backup-type entry in the ROM header, however, the
required type can be detected by ID strings in the ROM-image. Nintendo's tools
are automatically inserting these strings (as part of their library headers).
When using other tools, you may insert ID strings by hand.

ID Strings
The ID string must be located at a word-aligned memory location, the string
length should be a multiple of 4 bytes (padded with zero's).

  EEPROM_Vnnn    EEPROM 512 bytes or 8 Kbytes (4Kbit or 64Kbit)
  SRAM_Vnnn      SRAM 32 Kbytes (256Kbit)
  FLASH_Vnnn     FLASH 64 Kbytes (512Kbit) (ID used in older files)
  FLASH512_Vnnn  FLASH 64 Kbytes (512Kbit) (ID used in newer files)
  FLASH1M_Vnnn   FLASH 128 Kbytes (1Mbit)

For Nintendo's tools, "nnn" is a 3-digit library version number. When using
other tools, best keep it set to "nnn" rather than inserting numeric digits.

Notes
No$gba does auto-detect most backup types, even without ID strings, except for
128K FLASH (without ID "FLASH1M_Vnnn", the FLASH size defaults to 64K).
Ideally, for faster detection, the ID should be put into the first some bytes
of the ROM-image (ie. somewhere right after the ROM header).





  
  GBA Cart Backup SRAM/FRAM

SRAM - 32 KBytes (256Kbit) Lifetime: Depends on back-up battery
FRAM - 32 KBytes (256Kbit) Lifetime: 10,000,000,000 read/write per bit

Hyundai GM76V256CLLFW10 SRAM (Static RAM) (eg. F-Zero)
Fujitsu MB85R256 FRAM (Ferroelectric RAM) (eg. Warioware Twisted)

Addressing and Waitstates
SRAM/FRAM is mapped to E000000h-E007FFFh, it should be accessed with 8
waitstates (write a value of 3 into Bit0-1 of WAITCNT).

Databus Width
The SRAM/FRAM databus is restricted to 8 bits, it should be accessed by LDRB,
LDRSB, and STRB opcodes only.

Reading and Writing
Reading from SRAM/FRAM should be performed by code executed in WRAM only (but
not by code executed in ROM). There is no such restriction for writing.

Preventing Data Loss
The GBA SRAM/FRAM carts do not include a write-protect function (unlike older
8bit gameboy carts). This seems to be a problem and may cause data loss when a
cartridge is removed or inserted while the GBA is still turned on. As far as I
understand, this is not so much a hardware problem, but rather a software
problem, ie. theoretically you could remove/insert the cartridge as many times
as you want, but you should take care that your program does not crash (and
write blindly into memory).

Recommended Workaround
Enable the Gamepak Interrupt (it'll most likely get triggered when removing the
cartridge), and hang-up the GBA in an endless loop when your interrupt handler
senses a Gamepak IRQ. For obvious reason, your interrupt handler should be
located in WRAM, ie. not in the (removed) ROM cartridge. The handler should
process Gamepak IRQs at highest priority. Periods during which interrupts are

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: raw.sh <out-name> <first> <count> -- dump cand and ref frames [first, first+count) as gray raw
set -euo pipefail
S=/tmp/claude-1000/-var-www-html-test-projects-gba-trial-gba-emu/ec739230-fb4b-467b-9709-e53c38e370f4/scratchpad
name="$1"; first="$2"; count="$3"
last=$((first + count - 1))
for kind in cand ref; do
  src=/o/heartwrench-gameplay.$kind.mp4
  [ $kind = ref ] && src=/r/heartwrench-gameplay.ref.mp4
  docker run --rm --entrypoint /usr/bin/ffmpeg -v "$S/hwv/$name":/o -v "$S/triage5/out":/r:ro gba-eval-grader \
    -loglevel error -y -i $src -vf "select=between(n\,$first\,$last)" -vsync 0 -f rawvideo -pix_fmt gray /o/$kind-$first.raw
done

import sys

test = open(sys.argv[2]).read()
s = open(path).read()
old = "Region::Io => self.io_read16(io_offset(address)),\n            Region::Palette => read_le16"

assert s.count(head) == 1

accessed by the CPU only - restricted to bytewise 8bit transfers. The SRAM
region is supposed for as external FLASH backup memory, or for battery-backed
SRAM.

number of display-able OBJs though).

## Report: compat-timing, heartwrench-gameplay

Nothing I built beats the 0.577 video baseline. Following your rule, the graded branch `phase5/heartwrench-gameplay` has only the SRAM_V change and scores exactly the baseline. The prefetch buffer raises heartwrench audio from 0.554 to 0.928 but lowers video to 0.555. I kept it as one clean commit on a separate local branch so you can decide on it.

### 1. What I built and the commits

**Branch `phase5/heartwrench-gameplay`** (the one to merge):
- `0b3f768 feat(cart): detect SRAM_V and mirror 32 KiB SRAM`
  - In `/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-trial/gba-emu/.claude/worktrees/agent-a0a0b39470910a9fb/src/cart.rs`, a ROM with the `SRAM_V` string at a word-aligned offset gets 32 KiB of SRAM, mirrored across the save window (gbatek "GBA Cart Backup IDs" and "SRAM/FRAM"). Heartwrench has `SRAM_V113` at 0x3CB208.
  - Other ROMs keep the old 64 KiB.
  - It has a unit test. The 8-bit-only bus behaviour and the repeated byte on 16/32-bit reads were already correct in bus.rs.

**Branch `phase5/heartwrench-prefetch`** (not merged, kept for you):
- `a87eff9 feat(bus): Game Pak prefetch buffer for ROM opcode fetches`. This is on top of `0b3f768`, with the wip commit squashed into it.
- It follows gbatek "GBA GamePak Prefetch". The buffer holds up to 8 halfwords and fills one sequential access at a time while the Game Pak bus is idle: during CPU internal cycles and during accesses to other memory.
  - An opcode halfword already in the buffer costs 1 cycle.
  - One still being read costs only the cycles left on that read.
  - A miss is a normal access and restarts the buffer behind it.
- A unit test covers it.

### 2. Scores

| Test | Baseline (9848efd) | Final branch (SRAM_V only) | Prefetch branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| heartwrench-gameplay video | 0.5769 | 0.5769 | 0.5550 |
| heartwrench-gameplay audio | 0.5539 | 0.5539 | 0.9277 |
| spout-gameplay video / audio | 0.2857 / 0.1989 | same | same |
| The 16 procedural tests except tonc-snd1 | 1.0 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| tonc-snd1 video / audio | 0.9917 / 0.9815 | same | same |

- No smoke-set or procedural test dropped in any version. timer-reload and timer-start-stop stayed at 1.0.
- `cargo test` passes (127 tests on the final branch, 128 on the prefetch branch). The wasm build succeeds.

**First diverging frame** (first frame after 60 with per-frame error above 5):
- Before, and on the final branch: frame 237. After that, frames 1080-1110 are badly off (error up to 72), and the run breaks down from about frame 2430.
- With prefetch: frame 2488. Frames 0-2100 almost match, and the 1080 spike falls to about 10. Video still loses overall because the error from frame 2400 to 5700 is higher.

### 3. What I could not finish, guesses, and contract changes

**Why the game is timing-sensitive** (measured by running the replay natively):
- The game reads timer 2 and timer 3 about 1.15M times over the run and VCOUNT about 43k times. Its game logic depends on exact cycle timing.
- It reads the keypad once per frame at lines 172-224, well clear of the frame boundary, so input landing in the wrong frame is not the cause.
- The divergences come from frames where the game's work takes too long and it skips a frame ("lag frames"). The room load around frame 1060 is about 105k Thumb fetches per frame from ROM. With prefetch it finishes 2 frames earlier than Mesen; the baseline finishes later than Mesen.

**Evidence for the CPU-timing worker:**
- As a throwaway test, I added the missing branch refill cost (one extra sequential fetch per taken branch) inside the bus. With prefetch, frames 0-900 then matched Mesen exactly, and video was 0.5454, audio 0.7793.
- So prefetch needs the CPU side to charge branch refills (gbatek 2S+1N) before it can pay off. Neither change gets the full benefit alone.

**Guesses where gbatek is unclear** (in the prefetch commit):
- A ROM data read keeps the buffer, but the halfword being read is restarted as a non-sequential access. A version that cleared the buffer instead scored the same to 4 decimals.
- The buffer does not fill during the 1 cycle in which the CPU takes a buffered halfword. This brought the load end close to Mesen's (3 frames later in the native test).
- Buffer reads are always sequential, including at a 128 KiB boundary (marked `ponytail:`).

**Not done:**
- The "Prefetch Disable Bug" (an opcode fetch after an internal cycle costs N instead of S when prefetch is off).
- FLASH and EEPROM chips.

**Contract change needed:** prefetch needs the bus-idle time (CPU internal cycles), and the CPU only reports a total per step. As a workaround, the prefetch branch works out idle time from the PPU's position in the frame minus the access cycles charged. The cleaner fix is a `bus.idle(cycles)` call from the CPU, which means editing cpu/*.rs.

**Note on speed:** the prefetch build ran 1200 native frames in 10.0 s against 8.5 s before. The extra bus work is small; most of the cost is more halted steps, which are capped at 16 cycles each in cpu/mod.rs.

### 4. Decisions worth logging in NOTES.md
- 2026-11-05: Cart detects `SRAM_V` and uses 32 KiB mirrored SRAM (gbatek Backup IDs). Other ROMs keep 64 KiB until FLASH/EEPROM exist.
- 2026-11-05: Game Pak prefetch built but not merged. Heartwrench video went 0.577 to 0.555 and audio 0.554 to 0.928. Merge it once branch refill timing (2S+1N) is in the CPU; with a stand-in refill cost frames 0-900 matched exactly.
- 2026-11-05: Heartwrench reads timers 2/3 and VCOUNT constantly. Replay drift there is total-cycle sensitivity (lag frames), not key-poll phase.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
